articles.title: CRM Requirements for a Service Business: A Practical Template
articles.description: Define customer records, roles, workflows, integrations, and acceptance tests with a practical CRM requirements template for service businesses.
articles.question: What should a service business include in its CRM requirements?
articles.answer: A useful CRM requirements document explains the work people must complete, the information they need, and how you will check that the system supports both. Start with customer tasks, record relationships, responsibilities, and exceptions. Then translate those needs into a short set of observable tests before comparing products or asking for a development estimate.

articles.title: How to Connect a Website Form to a CRM Without Losing the Handoff
articles.description: Map website form fields to your CRM, distinguish repeat requests from duplicates, and test ownership, failures, and recovery before relying on the handoff.
articles.question: How do I connect a website form to a CRM and verify the handoff?
articles.answer: Connect a website form to a CRM by choosing a supported connection, mapping the submitted information to the right records, and defining who receives the next task. Then test whether each received inquiry becomes useful, assigned work—including requests from existing customers, repeated submissions, and interrupted connections.

articles.title: Custom CRM vs. Off-the-Shelf: Test Your Workflow Before You Build
articles.description: Compare configuring, extending, buying, and building a CRM using the same service-business tasks, ownership questions, and evidence of fit.
articles.question: Should a service business use a custom or off-the-shelf CRM?
articles.answer: Choose a custom CRM when important, demonstrated requirements remain difficult to satisfy through a suitable packaged product, configuration, or a focused integration—and when you can support the resulting system over time. Choose an existing product when it handles the essential work with acceptable constraints and operating responsibilities. The decision depends on the workflow you can prove, not whether your business considers itself unique.

articles.title: Contact Form Says “Sent,” but No Email Arrives: What to Check
articles.description: Trace missing contact-form emails from submission storage to the mailbox, gather useful evidence, and plan a retest after the problem is fixed.
articles.question: Why does my contact form say sent when no email arrives?
articles.answer: When a contact form appears to succeed but no email arrives, follow one labeled test request from the website to the receiving team. Check whether the submission was recorded, whether a notification was attempted, what the sending service reported, and where the receiving mailbox put the message. Repair the first verified failure, then repeat the complete test.

articles.title: Spreadsheet vs. CRM: When Should a Service Business Switch?
articles.description: Use five practical tasks to decide whether to keep your customer spreadsheet, improve the process, or move to a CRM. Includes a copyable comparison.
articles.question: When should a service business switch from a spreadsheet to a CRM?
articles.answer: A service business should consider switching from a spreadsheet to a CRM when its required customer tasks remain difficult to complete reliably after reasonable improvements to the sheet and working process. Look at ownership, next actions, history, related jobs, access, and handoffs. The number of contacts alone is not a useful switching rule.

articles.title: CRM Implementation Cost: Build a Budget Around Your Actual Scope
articles.description: Build a CRM budget covering setup, migration, integrations, recurring charges, and internal time, with two clearly hypothetical worked examples.
articles.question: What should a service business include in a CRM implementation budget?
articles.answer: A CRM implementation budget should include the work required to make the system useful, the recurring costs of operating it, and the staff time needed to adopt it. Start with the workflow, data, users, connections, and transition requirements. Then compare proposals against that same scope over a defined period.

articles.title: What Should an Automation Audit Include? Scope, Deliverables, and Cost
articles.description: Understand automation audit scope, evidence, deliverables, exclusions, and cost drivers. Use an acceptance rubric to compare a proposed engagement.
articles.question: What should an automation audit include and how should I compare its cost?
articles.answer: A useful automation audit shows how a defined piece of work happens today, what it costs to perform, where it breaks down, and which improvement deserves attention first. You should receive a plan you can evaluate, with evidence and assumptions clearly separated, rather than a list of software products to buy.

articles.title: CRM Migration Checklist: Keep Customer History and Open Work Intact
articles.description: Plan a CRM migration around identifiers, relationships, owners, open tasks, and recovery decisions, with a fictional rehearsal and reconciliation checklist.
articles.question: How do I plan a CRM migration without losing customer context or open work?
articles.answer: A CRM migration needs to preserve the relationships and open work that make the records useful. Define what will move, map identifiers and ownership, rehearse representative cases, and reconcile the result before the team depends on the new system. A successful file upload is one step in that process, not the acceptance test.

articles.title: How to Track Website Inquiries Through to Qualified Leads
articles.description: Separate browser events, received inquiries, and qualified leads. Reconcile counts with a worked example and preserve uncertainty in source attribution.
articles.question: How do I track website inquiries through to qualified leads?
articles.answer: Track website inquiries by defining separate stages: a visitor's contact action, a received request, a distinct inquiry, a qualification decision, and a business outcome. Give each stage a reliable evidence source, test the path, and reconcile the counts. A button click or form event should not stand in for all five stages.

articles.title: What to Do When an Automation Fails: A Recovery Checklist
articles.description: Find the last confirmed business result, choose a safe recovery action, and reconcile outstanding work using an automation incident checklist.
articles.question: How do I recover a failed automation without repeating completed actions?
articles.answer: When an automation fails, first establish which work is affected and which actions already completed. Then choose how to finish the missing work without repeating completed records, messages, or other changes. Confirm the result in the receiving system before treating the incident as resolved.

articles.title: Client Portal vs. CRM: Which Tasks Belong Where?
articles.description: Map customer access and internal CRM responsibilities, assess existing portal features, and define permissions with a practical service-business example.
articles.question: Does my service business need a client portal, a CRM, or both?
articles.answer: A CRM helps your team coordinate customer information and work. A client portal gives customers access to selected information and actions. You may need one, both, or the portal already included in your existing software. Start with the task that is failing, then decide where it belongs.

articles.title: AI or Rules-Based Automation? Test Your Inquiry Workflow First
articles.description: Compare rules and bounded AI tasks using 12 fictional inquiries, explicit unknowns, expected outcomes, and a reusable evaluation worksheet.
articles.question: Should I use AI or rules to route and interpret customer inquiries?
articles.answer: Use rules when the information and next action are explicit: a selected service, a known location, or a request already assigned to someone. Consider AI for a bounded interpretation task, such as organizing a free-text message for review. Compare both approaches on the same examples before deciding whether the additional work is worthwhile.
